Every graphics setting will, strictly speaking, either lower graphical fidelity or decrease framerate. The key is to find out which ones are most important to you, or to weigh their effect vs the framerate they take That is largely up to preference, some people love having anti-aliasing to the max, but I prefer having it off or very low, for instance. Likewise I will go through and disable everything before dropping my resolution, but some people prefer to drop the resolution so they can keep all the graphical effects. I'd suggest starting with a fairly intensive game and playing with all the toggles and a FPS counter. You will learn over time which settings you like and which ones you don't, or which ones you just don't notice yet seem to eat up 20fps. I would personally start with anti aliasing, followed by post processing and lighting effects. I don't like most of these, and they tend to be big drains on your frames. Reflections can be a pretty big hit to your framerate for fairly marginal benefit also.

I work in digital journalism and have done for the past decade. I wanted to be a journalist but didnâĢĻt want to get saddled with student debt for a career I didnâĢĻt think would be feasible. You donâĢĻt need to study and get a degree to be a journalist. You just need to start finding stories and doing the work. A good shortcut is sending yourself to a place where there is a lot of news and where youâĢĻre passionate about the place, people, culture and learn the language. It doesnâĢĻt have to be a foreign country, though thatâĢĻs what I did, but a place where there are few other journalists covering an important story. Pitch to news organizations that you like. Look up who the editor is. Try to pitch to them directly when you have a specific story idea. Learn the digital skills. Teach yourself to film, photograph, edit video and start your own website. You need to be a self starter. You will have to freelance for a while before anyone will hire you as staff. And frankly, in this climate, you need to be mentally prepared to get laid off and be freelance again even if you someday manage to secure a cushy staff position. IâĢĻm a bit worried that you say you donâĢĻt make and maintain contacts easily. Contacts are everything; not just in getting hired, but in being able to find and interview people for your stories. Contacts are key to finding experts and being able to quickly negotiate access to your story. I donâĢĻt think anyone can just teach you to be a journalist. You can learn the skills, but at the end of the day, there are so many journalism grads for so few paid positions. You have to think about what more you bring to the profession. Do you have a speciality? How can you distinguish yourself? A major in something practical with a journalism minor is sensible if you really feel school is the way to go.

I think the problem in this scenario is the fact that some people lack opportunity. What if you grow up in a place that does not offer free education? What if you grow in a place without a good government to help you? What if you grow up in a family that can not afford to send you to school? There are many countries that do not offer free education or good education. There are also countries like Iran that discriminate against women and it becomes very difficult for them to get an education. However, I think your post focused around America, so I will delve into that subject. In America, your point makes a good deal more sense. There is welfare, free education, libraries, and scholarships. Colleges are always willing to give scholarships to hardworking poor people because they get so few of them. However even with all of this, the system does not always work. Many public schools quite frankly, suck. The good ones tend to be in richer neighborhoods or nice suburbs. The ones in the poor neighborhoods have apathetic teachers, even more apathetic parents and students, are deep in debt, and have extremely bad administration. There are classes where students will not learn much at all. I am in through an urban public highschool with largely poor black kids. Most of them have no supportive family like yours, did not have a good beginning in education when they were to young to realize that education might be good for them, and the school system doesn't do anything about it. They get kicked out if they get bad grades, but no one actually stops them from getting bad grades or encourages them to get good ones. At this point, they are too far behind to easily catch up on their own without adult support. Most of the teachers in the non-advanced classes are the worse ones, the better ones being assigned to the advanced classes. I think the thing that makes it hardest to succeed is having bad parents, particularly uneducated, poor, and demotivating ones. When a child is very young they do not know any better and only try as hard in school as their parents make them. By the time they are old enough to understand this, it is too late for them to catch up without help and most of the time, that help never comes. The key difference in your scenario is that your parents were supportive. I think you are underestimating how huge of an impact that has.
